t: Count Good Meals — Counting Pairs That Sum to Powers of Two
o: A good meal is an unordered pair of two different food items whose deliciousness values add up to a power of two; items are distinguished by index, so equal values still form pairs. In Example 1 (`[1,3,5,7,9]`) the qualifying pairs are (1,3)→4, (1,7)→8, (3,5)→8 and (7,9)→16 — 4 meals. Example 2 (`[1,1,1,3,3,3,7]`) shows multiplicity: (1,1) contributes 3 pairs, (1,3) contributes 3×3 = 9, and (1,7) contributes 3, totaling 15. Values reach $2^{20}$, so any pair's sum is at most $2^{21}$ — only 22 candidate sums exist. Checking all pairs is O(n²) ≈ 10^10 operations, too slow for n = 10^5; keeping a hash map of how often each value has appeared so far lets us, for every item d and every power $2^p$, add the count of its complement $2^p - d$ in constant time — O(22) per item overall.
k: There are at most 22 target sums: each value is at most $2^{20}$, so a pair sums to $2^p$ with $0 \le p \le 21$ (note 0 is not a power of two).
Processing items left to right and counting only complements seen SO FAR counts each unordered pair exactly once and handles d + d = power pairs automatically.
Apply the 10^9+7 modulus to the running pair counter only; the occurrence counts themselves must stay exact.

a.i: Enumerate all index pairs i < j and test whether the sum is a power of two. A positive integer s is a power of two exactly when s & (s−1) == 0, which avoids even enumerating the 22 targets. Simple and obviously correct, but quadratic.
s: Loop i from 0 to n−1 and j from i+1 to n−1.
Count the pair if s > 0 and s & (s − 1) == 0.
a.t: O(n²) — every unordered pair is examined once

a.n: Approach 2: One-Pass Hash Map over the 22 Target Powers
a.i: Sweep the array once, maintaining cnt[v] = how many times value v has already been seen. When handling item d, every previous occurrence of $2^p - d$ forms a good meal with it, for each of the 22 powers; summing those counts adds each pair exactly once because only the later index does the looking up. Pairs of equal values (d + d being a power of two) come out naturally from earlier occurrences of d itself.
s: Initialize an empty hash map cnt and an answer accumulator.
For each item d: for every p in 0..21 add cnt[2^p − d] (missing keys contribute 0) to the answer.
After probing all 22 powers, increment cnt[d].
a.t: O(22 · n) — each item probes 22 powers in a hash map
a.sp: O(n) — occurrence counts for distinct values seen so far

w: Present the hash-map sweep as your main solution; the "only 22 possible sums" insight is the crux interviewers want to hear. Common pitfalls: double-counting pairs (increment counts only AFTER probing), forgetting that (d, d) meals need two separate occurrences, treating 0 as a power of two (sums must be 1, 2, 4, ...), stopping powers at $2^{20}$ instead of $2^{21}$, and applying the modulus to intermediate occurrence counts instead of just the answer. Edge cases: arrays heavy on equal values (pair counts grow combinatorially — hence the modulus), zeros pairing with nothing since 0+0=0 is not a power of two. Follow-ups: extend to triples summing to a power of two, or support a stream where you report the running pair count after every insertion.
